Its exact English expression depends on the surrounding words, so the word should be understood as part of the larger phrase rather than isolated from it. It occurs 58 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across 57 verses, including passages in Genesis, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Kings, Job, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hosea, and Malachi.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “morning,” the early part of the day after night. It functions as a time reference in sentences, marking when something happens, is observed, or is commanded. It is used broadly across the Old Testament, appearing 214 times, from Genesis through Zephaniah. Scripture uses it in ordinary descriptions of time as well as in accounts of worship, instruction, speech, and significant events. Its precise force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage.

This word refers to a den, especially the enclosed place where lions are kept. It functions as a noun naming that place rather than an action or quality. In its Hebrew Bible usage, it appears ten times, all within Daniel 6, where the den is associated with the lions and with the sentence imposed on Daniel. Its precise force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains a den or lions’ pit.

This Hebrew noun means “wall,” referring to a structure that forms a boundary or enclosure. It is used twice in the Old Testament corpus, and both recorded renderings are “wall.” The word can therefore describe a physical barrier or dividing structure, while the surrounding verse determines its particular setting and purpose. Its occurrences are found in Proverbs 24:31 and Ezekiel 42:10, but the word’s basic meaning remains the same: a constructed boundary that separates, encloses, or helps define a space.

This Hebrew word refers to “berries,” using a plural noun for the fruit itself. It occurs once in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, in Isaiah 17:6. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise role in that verse must be understood from the wider context. Its meaning remains focused and concrete: it identifies berries rather than an action, quality, person, or abstract idea.

Hemam is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Hemam” in English. It is not presented here with an ordinary descriptive definition, so its meaning is chiefly its role as the name of a person. This word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Genesis 36:22. Without the verse text or a broader lexical definition, no further sense should be assigned beyond identifying Hemam as the person’s name.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “slaughter,” describing the killing of people as an event or outcome. It occurs five times in the Old Testament, appearing in Esther, Proverbs, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. Its uses are associated with people being killed or slain, while the precise force in any particular verse depends on that verse’s surrounding words and passage. The word therefore points to a severe act of killing rather than to an ordinary death or a general reference to harm.

This Hebrew word refers to “companions”—people who are associated with someone as close fellows or partners. In Daniel, it is used for Daniel’s associates, appearing three times in Daniel 2:13, 17, and 18. The word therefore points to people connected with one another in a shared situation, rather than to a solitary individual. Its normal sense is relational: those who stand alongside another person as companions.

This Hebrew word means "terror"—a condition of dread or fear that overwhelms a person. It is a rare word, occurring once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 19:17. Since the available biblical usage is limited to that single occurrence and no surrounding verse text is provided here, its exact force in that passage must be understood from the wider context. Its central idea remains terror: an experience that causes deep alarm rather than ordinary concern.

Hatipha is a personal name, rendered "Hatipha." It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this name occurs twice: once in Ezra 2:54 and once in Nehemiah 7:56. Because no broader lexical definition is available, its meaning is best understood as the person’s name, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific historical setting. The name is preserved consistently in the English renderings associated with both occurrences.

Hamulites is a plural group name, identifying people collectively rather than naming one individual. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Numbers 26:21, and its English rendering is “Hamulites.” Because no short definition or verse text is available here, the safest plain-language understanding is the name of a people or family group. Its exact relationship to the surrounding census list must be read from Numbers 26.

Hosah is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The Hebrew word appears five times in the Old Testament, and each occurrence is rendered “Hosah.” It is found once in Joshua and four times in 1 Chronicles, functioning as a person’s name in those passages. The supplied references identify where this name occurs, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain each individual mention.

The surrounding SEE connections associate the name with birth or begetting and genealogy, so it functions as a person’s name in a family record. The available passage evidence does not provide a broader lexical meaning beyond this identification.

Hatticon is a Hebrew proper name referring to a specific place. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Ezekiel 47:16. As a named location, it identifies a geographic point rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. The surrounding passage is needed to explain its exact role in Ezekiel’s list of places, but the word itself functions as a place-name: “Hatticon.”

One occurrence is rendered “dung,” and the other appears in a speech setting involving the same subject. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew verb means “drive.” It describes an action directed toward another person, expressing the forceful movement or removal of someone from a place. The word occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Daniel. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central idea remains the act of driving someone away or out. This is a limited biblical usage, so the normal sense is best kept closely tied to that basic action.

e.t: This word is the personal name “Jehoash,” a king of Judah in the Old Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than a general description or action word. The name appears 17 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within 2 Kings, referring to the same named royal figure across those passages. Its exact significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding account, but its ordinary lexical function is simply to identify Jehoash.

This Hebrew word means “genealogy.” It refers to a recorded family line or lineage, especially when people are identified and counted according to their ancestry. In the Old Testament, it is used in genealogical lists and records concerning Israel’s families. The word occurs 20 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from 1 Chronicles through Nehemiah, showing its regular role in describing family descent and ancestry rather than a personal name or isolated individual. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding record.

Jeconiah is a personal name, referring to a king of Judah and to the same named individual in genealogical and historical records. It functions as a person’s name rather than as a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. This Hebrew name appears seven times in the Old Testament corpus, including records in 1 Chronicles, Esther, and Jeremiah. The English rendering consistently identifies the person as “Jeconiah.” Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word is a personal name rendered “Jeshebeab.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 24:13. Since no separate lexical definition is provided, its meaning is best understood as the proper name itself, not expanded into an unsupported translation or symbolic meaning.

Ithmah is a Hebrew personal name, not a common word that describes an action, object, or quality. It refers to a man named Ithmah in the Old Testament record. This name occurs once in the Hebrew Bible corpus, at 1 Chronicles 11:46, and its English rendering is consistently “Ithmah.” The available information does not provide a separate lexical definition, so the name itself is the meaning readers can safely recognize here.

This Hebrew word describes being “burned,” referring to the effect of fire on someone or something. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Proverbs 6:28 and once in Isaiah 43:2. In ordinary sentence use, it functions as the action or condition of burning rather than naming the fire itself. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to the land around a town or settlement, commonly rendered “suburbs” or “pasture.” It describes space set apart beyond the built-up area, especially land connected with towns given to the Levites. In the Old Testament it occurs 115 times, with its use concentrated in passages describing the lands and open areas assigned around Israelite cities. Its precise extent depends on context.

This Hebrew word means “measured.” It functions as a verb describing the act of determining or marking the extent of something. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Habakkuk 3:6. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that verse cannot be described beyond this basic action. The word’s single occurrence makes it relatively rare, while its recorded meaning gives a clear central idea: something is measured.

This Hebrew noun means “profit,” referring to what results from work or effort. It appears three times in the Old Testament, in Proverbs and Ecclesiastes. The word can identify the outcome being sought through diligent activity, while its precise force in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding context. Its uses therefore center on the idea of profit as the result or advantage connected with human labor and plans.

This Hebrew word is a rare term whose precise meaning cannot be established from the available lexical information. It occurs only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezra 1:9. Because no definition, gloss, or approved meaning clue is available, it would be misleading to assign an English meaning or describe its specific role in that verse. Its meaning must therefore be determined from the verse’s full wording and surrounding context.

This Hebrew verb expresses the idea of “prepared.” It describes an action in which someone prepares something or arranges it for a purpose. The word occurs 28 times in the Old Testament, so it is used across several kinds of passages rather than belonging to only one setting. Its exact force—what is being prepared and for what purpose—depends on the sentence and its surrounding context.

This Hebrew verb means “commit,” expressing the act of handing something or someone over to another authority or responsibility. In its two Old Testament occurrences, it appears in Numbers 31:5 and 31:16, so its recorded use is concentrated in one passage rather than spread broadly across the Hebrew Bible. The word functions as an action: it describes what someone does by placing something into another’s charge or control. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word means “little.” It functions as a descriptive word, marking something as limited in size, extent, or degree. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Daniel 8:9. Because the word appears only there and the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the surrounding context. Its basic sense remains a designation of something little.

It can also appear in accounts involving death and personal loss.

Thus, it points not merely to an institution, but to the authority and rule exercised by a ruler. Its precise force in each verse depends on the surrounding context.

Its clearest supported meaning is therefore “psalteries,” while the surrounding sentence determines how the instrument relates to the action described. Occurrences connect it especially with speech and giving praise.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “cart,” referring to a wheeled vehicle used to carry people or things. It appears 25 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including accounts of carts being provided, given, or moved. Its normal function is as the object or thing involved in an action, rather than the action itself. The word therefore points to a practical means of transport in the passages where it occurs.

This Hebrew word means “rejoice”: to express gladness, celebrate, or exult. It describes an outward response of joy rather than merely a quiet inner feeling. In the Old Testament, it is used in statements of praise and confidence, including rejoicing connected with God and triumph over trouble or opposition. The word occurs eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing especially in Psalms and Proverbs. Its precise emphasis in any verse depends on the surrounding words, but its central idea is active, expressed joy.

This Hebrew noun means “humility,” describing a modest, lowly posture rather than pride or self-exaltation. In its four Old Testament occurrences, it is associated with the wisdom that comes before honor, the proper attitude of a person whose heart has been humbled, and the way of those who seek the LORD. The word names an inward quality or disposition, not merely an outward act. Its related use with meekness in Zephaniah reinforces the sense of willingly taking a low place before God.

This Hebrew name occurs 15 times in the Old Testament, appearing most often in Genesis and also in Joshua and 2 Chronicles. Its role in a specific passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the word itself functions as a person’s name.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “pledge”: something given as security for a promised payment or obligation. It functions as an object in speech about giving and receiving such security. The word occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Genesis 38, where its use is connected with giving and with a promised exchange. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is a pledge held as assurance that an obligation will be fulfilled.

This Hebrew word means “here,” pointing to a particular place or location. It commonly identifies where someone or something is, or directs attention to a place being discussed. As a location word, its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence: it may indicate where a person is standing, where an action should occur, or where something can be found. It occurs 82 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing regular use across the biblical narrative and prophetic books. The word is especially frequent in Ezekiel, but its central meaning remains a simple reference to place.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name, referring to Esar-Haddon. It appears six times in the Old Testament corpus, across three verses: 2 Kings 19:37, Ezra 4:2, and Isaiah 37:38. English renderings preserve the two parts of the name as “Esar” and “Haddon.” The word functions as a specific designation rather than a general description or action. Its occurrences are connected with speech and with worship or bowing, but the name itself identifies the person being mentioned.

This Hebrew word means “fruitful.” It functions as the predicate of a statement, describing someone or something as producing fruit or showing fruitfulness. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Hosea 13:15. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the condition of being fruitful. It is not a general label for fruit itself; it describes the fruitful state or result.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a covered carrier or litter, something used to carry a person or load. Its translated sense is associated with “covered” and “litters,” indicating an enclosed or sheltered means of transport rather than an action or abstract idea. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Leviticus 11:29, Numbers 7:3, and Isaiah 66:20. The exact English wording can differ by passage, but the central idea remains a covered carrying vehicle or conveyance.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Zalmunna.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. The name occurs twelve times in the Hebrew Old Testament, mostly in Judges 8 and once in Psalm 83. Because it functions as a proper name, its meaning for readers is chiefly the person it designates, while the surrounding passage supplies the details about that person.

This Hebrew word means “beside,” describing a position or place next to something or someone. It functions as a word of location, showing where a person or object is situated in relation to another. It occurs 61 times in the Old Testament, so its basic sense is used across many settings rather than being limited to one passage. The surrounding words determine exactly what stands beside what in each verse, but the central idea remains placement alongside another person or thing.

This Hebrew word refers to “goats.” It is a noun naming these animals, and its recorded use is limited to one occurrence in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Ezra 6:17. The word appears in a list of animals associated with an offering, so its basic meaning identifies the kind of animal being presented. The surrounding verse provides the fuller significance of that offering, but the word itself specifically denotes goats.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to "thorns"—sharp, prickly growths that can hinder people, damage crops, or be used as a means of punishment. It is a noun describing a physical thing, and its Old Testament uses consistently carry this ordinary sense. The word occurs 12 times in the Hebrew Bible, from Genesis through Hosea, including passages involving fields, fire, conflict, and imagery of stubborn or ungodly people. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

“Kezia” functions as a personal name. It identifies a woman named in Job 42:14 and is not presented here as an ordinary action, quality, or object word. This Hebrew word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Job 42:14. Its role is therefore chiefly to identify the person bearing this name; the surrounding verse supplies the fuller context for her place in the passage.

This Hebrew word means “city,” referring to an inhabited urban place. It functions as a noun and is used consistently with that meaning across its five Old Testament occurrences. The word appears once in Job and four times in Proverbs, where it can be spoken of as a place connected with public life and community. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a city.

This Hebrew word expresses being unable to settle or find rest. It functions as a verb, describing restless movement or a failure to become calm and settled rather than naming a fixed object or person. In its Old Testament use, the idea can involve seeking a place of rest, enduring continual disturbance, or describing something that lasts only briefly. It occurs 13 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its precise force depends on the sentence in which it appears.

It is a Hebrew noun referring to “dromedaries,” the plural animals named in Esther 8:10. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word occurs only once, so its basic meaning is narrow and concrete rather than a broad idea or action. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies these animals being mentioned there.

This Hebrew verb means “drop.” It describes something falling downward, especially in the Old Testament’s imagery of rain or water coming from above. The word appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Job, Psalms, Proverbs, and Isaiah. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is said to drop and where it comes from. In Isaiah 45:8, it functions as the action connecting God with what comes from heaven to earth.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “tribes,” naming the distinct tribal groups among Israel. It commonly identifies a people-group as a recognized unit, especially when tribes are counted, gathered, given land, or addressed together. The word occurs 190 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that this is an established term for Israel’s tribal divisions rather than an occasional description. Its exact significance in any verse depends on how that tribe or tribal group functions in the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew noun means “fulness” and names a condition of being full rather than an action or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 16:49. Its role is to identify fullness as a state or condition. The surrounding verse determines what this fullness concerns and how it functions in that statement, but the word itself points to the condition named by “fulness.”

This Hebrew word refers to “walls,” naming the structures that enclose or protect a place. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within three verses of Ezra 4:12–16. Its repeated use in this short passage keeps the meaning focused on walls rather than on a broader figurative idea. The word’s precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is clear: walls.

Shiza is a Hebrew personal name, preserved as “Shiza” rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, at 1 Chronicles 11:42, and the English renderings retain the name in that form. Because no lexical definition or surrounding verse text is available here, the secure meaning-level explanation is its naming function: it identifies a person in the biblical record, not a general quality, action, or object.

This Hebrew word is a rare term whose precise meaning cannot be determined from the available lexical information. It appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 31:21. No gloss, short definition, or English rendering is available here, so assigning a specific meaning would go beyond the evidence. Its role belongs to the wording of that single verse, but the surrounding verse text is not provided for further clarification.

This Hebrew action word means "come." It functions as the sentence’s predicate, expressing the action of coming toward or arriving at a place or person. Its ordinary sense remains consistent across its 16 occurrences in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing especially in Ezra and Daniel. The word can describe people being summoned or arriving, but its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

Bavai is a personal name, functioning as a designation for an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 3:18, and is rendered “Bavai” in the available English rendering. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, this entry identifies the word’s normal lexical function, not the individual’s role or significance in that passage. The name’s single occurrence makes it a rare Hebrew word in the biblical corpus.
